title: Course Schedule
description: Brute force to optimized: DFS with three-state cycle detection versus Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees).

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given numCourses and a list of prerequisite pairs [a, b] (meaning course b must be taken before course a), return true if it is possible to finish all courses.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Model each course as a node, and each prerequisite pair [a, b] as a directed edge from b to a (b must come before a). All courses can be finished exactly when this directed graph has NO CYCLE, since a cycle would mean a group of courses that all (indirectly) require each other, an impossible situation.

blocks.title: Analogy: Scheduling Tasks With Prerequisites, Detecting an Impossible Circular Dependency
blocks.text: Picture scheduling tasks where some tasks require others to be done first. If task A requires B, B requires C, and C circles back to requiring A, none of these three tasks could ever actually be started, an impossible circular dependency. Detecting whether any such cycle exists tells whether the whole schedule is achievable.

blocks.caption: All courses finishable exactly when the prerequisite graph has no cycle

blocks.text: Result: false (course 1 needs course 0, and course 0 needs course 1, a cycle).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Build a directed graph where an edge from b to a means "b must be completed before a".

Observation 2: Compute the IN-DEGREE of every node (how many prerequisites it still has); a node with in-degree 0 can be taken immediately, with no unmet prerequisites.

Observation 3: Repeatedly process nodes with in-degree 0 (Kahn's algorithm): removing such a node conceptually "completes" it, decrementing the in-degree of everything it points to, potentially freeing up NEW zero-in-degree nodes.

Observation 4: If EVERY node eventually gets processed this way, the graph has no cycle, and all courses can be finished; if some nodes are NEVER reached (their in-degree never drops to 0), a cycle exists among them, making completion impossible.
This leads to Kahn's algorithm: a BFS-style topological sort processing zero-in-degree nodes, checking if all nodes get processed.
Use DFS, tracking which nodes are currently on the ACTIVE recursion path (the current path being explored); revisiting a node still on this active path indicates a cycle.
Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking three states per node during DFS correctly detects cycles via the "in progress" marker.

This requires careful state management (unvisited, in-progress, done) to avoid subtle bugs; Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees) achieves the same result with a conceptually simpler queue-based process.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(courses plus prerequisites), similar to Kahn's algorithm.
Space: O(courses) recursion depth.
Limitation: Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees) achieves the same complexity with simpler iterative bookkeeping, avoiding the three-state DFS tracking.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build the adjacency list and in-degree array from the prerequisites. Initialize a queue with every node having in-degree 0. Process the queue: dequeue a node, count it as completed, and for each course it points to, decrement that course's in-degree; if it reaches 0, enqueue it. After the queue empties, check if the total completed count equals numCourses; if so, no cycle exists and all courses can be finished.
Use Kahn's algorithm: BFS processing zero-in-degree nodes, checking if all nodes get processed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["Initial in-degrees","course 0: 0, course 1: 1"],["Queue starts with course 0","process it, count=1, decrement course 1's in-degree to 0, enqueue it"],["Process course 1","count=2, equals numCourses, all courses finishable"]]}

blocks.text: A node can only ever reach in-degree 0 (and thus be processed) once ALL of its prerequisites have themselves already been processed; if the graph is a DAG (no cycle), every node eventually reaches in-degree 0 through this chain reaction, and the total count of processed nodes reaches numCourses. If a cycle exists, every node WITHIN that cycle can never reach in-degree 0 (each depends circularly on another in the same cycle), so the final count falls short, correctly signaling impossibility.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(courses plus prerequisites).
Space: O(courses plus prerequisites) for the adjacency list and in-degree array.

items: Reversing the edge direction (from a to b instead of from b to a), inverting the entire in-degree computation.

Forgetting to check the FINAL processed count against numCourses, instead assuming the queue simply emptying means success (it does not, if a cycle exists, some nodes are simply never enqueued at all).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "some tasks require others first, can everything be completed?", think: cycle detection via topological sort (Kahn's algorithm or DFS).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the DFS and Kahn's algorithm approaches cost O(courses plus prerequisites); Kahn's algorithm is generally considered the more straightforward implementation.

items: Pattern: topological sort / cycle detection in a directed graph.
Core Idea: repeatedly process zero-in-degree nodes; all courses are finishable exactly when every node eventually gets processed.
Time: O(courses plus prerequisites) for both approaches.
Space: O(courses) recursion depth for DFS, O(courses plus prerequisites) for Kahn's algorithm.
Most Important Observation: a cycle means some nodes never reach in-degree 0, directly detectable via the final processed count.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, foundational medium-level graph problem.
One line memory trick: process zero in-degree nodes; a cycle leaves some unprocessed.
